summary:
The Burmese Peacock Softshell, a rare and ancient-looking turtle found only in the rivers of Myanmar, once glided through the currents of the Ayeyarwady, Chindwin, and Sittaung — great waterways that shaped civilizations. Soft-shelled and unhurried, it was a creature built for patience, slow to mature and slow to breed, carrying within it a rhythm entirely out of step with the pace of human hunger.

That slowness became its vulnerability. Harvested for food trade, its eggs taken from riverbanks, its habitat fractured by gold mining, dynamite fishing, and surging boat traffic, the species has lost an estimated 80% of its population over ninety years. It lingers now in low numbers, a quiet disappearance unfolding in muddy water.
